Name: selection_rule_forbidden_transition_probe
Title: Bright or Dark? Testing Whether Molecular/Materials Foundation Models Represent Symmetry-Based Optical Selection Rules, Not Just the Energy Gap
Short Hypothesis: Whether an electronic transition absorbs light is set by an exactly-known symmetry mechanism—optical selection rules (Laporte/parity, spin, and orbital-symmetry rules)—that determines the oscillator strength (bright vs dark) largely independently of the energy-gap size: two molecules can have nearly identical HOMO-LUMO gaps yet one is intensely absorbing and the other symmetry-forbidden (dark). We hypothesize that if a molecular/materials foundation model represents this selection-rule mechanism rather than treating optical activity as a monotone function of the energy gap, then (a) transition brightness (oscillator strength) is decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from the gap, (b) a symmetry-breaking counterfactual—a small distortion that lowers molecular symmetry and turns a forbidden (dark) transition allowed (bright) at nearly-fixed gap—shifts the internal brightness signal accordingly, whereas a symmetry-preserving perturbation of matched magnitude does not, and (c) steering a recovered 'allowedness' direction causally reshapes predicted absorption without changing the gap. The forbidden-vs-allowed symmetry counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that gap correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) ML for optical/excited-state properties—TD-DFT surrogate models, oscillator-strength and UV-Vis spectrum predictors (e.g., message-passing and transformer models on QM8/QM9-spectra, Oled/optical datasets), and excited-state foundation models—are trained to predict excitation energies and intensities but are judged by regression error, not by whether they internalize the selection-rule mechanism. (2) Interpretability of chemistry/atomistic foundation models—SAE studies on chemistry FMs, 'Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers' (2025), MoleX (2024), and periodic-law/spin-state probes—recover substructure/element/valence features validated against ground/scalar annotations, none of which concern excited-state symmetry. Physics/interpretability work recovers and steers single scalar quantities (energy, vorticity) but never the parity/spin symmetry that decides whether a transition is bright or dark. Crucially, no work tests whether a foundation model internally represents optical selection rules—the symmetry mechanism separating oscillator strength from the energy gap—whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a symmetry-breaking counterfactual to arbitrate mechanism vs gap correlation. Because bright transitions also tend to have accessible gaps in typical data, correlation-based benchmarks cannot separate the two. Our brightness-beyond-gap probe, forbidden-vs-allowed symmetry counterfactual, and causal allowedness steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, distinct from the chirality (pseudoscalar) and spin-state probes in also targeting the parity/orbital-symmetry selection mechanism of excited states. Positioned against three method families: intensity-regression benchmarks judge output error, SAE and feature cataloguing on chemistry FMs recover static substructure, and geometric sensitivity analysis varies distortion magnitude, none holding the gap fixed while flipping only symmetry as our counterfactual does.
Abstract: Whether a molecule absorbs light at a given color is governed not by the size of its energy gap alone but by an exactly-known symmetry mechanism: optical selection rules. Parity (Laporte), spin, and orbital-symmetry rules decide whether an electronic transition is allowed (bright, large oscillator strength) or forbidden (dark, vanishing intensity), and this can flip a transition from dark to bright with a tiny symmetry-lowering distortion that barely changes the gap. This makes selection rules an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether molecular/materials foundation models learn excited-state symmetry or merely a gap-to-intensity correlate. We probe pretrained molecular foundation models and optical-property predictors on datasets with computed oscillator strengths and excitation energies (e.g., QM8, QM9-spectra, and curated symmetric/near-symmetric molecule sets). First, a brightness-beyond-gap probe: is transition oscillator strength decodable from internal representations beyond what the energy gap predicts, along a distinct axis? Second, and most decisively, a symmetry-breaking counterfactual: we apply a small distortion that lowers molecular symmetry and turns a forbidden transition allowed at nearly-fixed gap, versus a matched symmetry-preserving distortion that keeps it dark, and test whether the internal brightness signal responds to the symmetry change, not the gap; a gap-correlate model responds identically. Third, causal allowedness steering reshapes predicted absorption without shifting the gap. Metrics quantify a brightness-beyond-gap index, a symmetry-break-vs-preserve causal asymmetry, and an intensity-error failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed optical-property models represent selection rules or are blind to them—critical for photochemistry and materials discovery. The novelty is twofold and explicitly separated: a representation finding (brightness on an axis distinct from the gap) and a causal mechanism test (the symmetry-breaking counterfactual), in an excited-state selection-rule setting no prior probe has entered. Beyond scientific insight into what optical-property models learn, this is a practical model audit: excited-state-ML, photochemistry, and mechanistic-interpretability researchers would run it before deploying a model for dark/bright-state design, e.g. OLED-emitter and forbidden-transition screening, where a model that treats intensity as a gap correlate will mis-rank symmetry-forbidden dark states. A positive result licenses such screening; a negative result flags a specific, correctable blind spot.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- transition brightness is decodable along an axis distinct from the energy gap): Tests clause (a): oscillator strength (brightness) is decodable from internal representations on an axis distinct from the HOMO-LUMO gap. Data: QM8 (an existing set used as is; 21,786 molecules with TD-DFT excitation energies and oscillator strengths for the lowest transitions) plus QM9-spectra; from these we curate a diagnostic subset of ~500 high-symmetry / near-symmetric molecules (centrosymmetric species, symmetric aromatics) that host Laporte/parity-forbidden transitions, chosen because forbidden-vs-allowed pairs at matched gap are the decisive cases. For each low-lying transition we record excitation energy (gap), oscillator strength f, spin/symmetry-forbidden class, and point group. Model: a 3D atomistic FM (Uni-Mol or MACE latents, ~few-x10M parameters) and a SMILES/graph FM (ChemBERTa-2, ~46-125M parameters), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: ridge (f, gap) and logistic (forbidden vs allowed), L2 via 5-fold CV, standardized features, 5 seeds with scaffold-grouped splits (no molecular scaffold shared across splits); report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a gap-only baseline predicting f from excitation energy; (ii) Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index = probe R^2 for f from the representation minus the gap-only R^2, after residualizing the gap-predictable component; (iii) the angle between the recovered gap direction and the recovered brightness direction. Decisive metric first: Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 (95% bootstrap CI over held-out scaffolds excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) AND gap-vs-brightness axis angle >= 60 degrees (distinct axes), holding on the matched-gap forbidden/allowed subset. Refute: Index <= 0.02 and angle <= 20 degrees (brightness collapses onto the gap). Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 or angle 20-60 degrees (stated before the data): unresolved -- some gap-independent brightness signal but not a cleanly separate axis; we report it and do not treat clause (a) as established. A negative result means the model encodes intensity as a gap correlate, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a symmetry-breaking edit brightens a forbidden transition while a matched symmetry-preserving edit does not): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: ~150 centrosymmetric/high-symmetry molecules from the Experiment-1 diagnostic subset each hosting a parity-forbidden dark transition; for every molecule we construct one symmetry-breaking distortion (lowers the point group; by selection rules turns the transition allowed at nearly-fixed gap) and one symmetry-preserving control distortion at matched RMSD (transition stays dark). Both edits are constructed and verified by recomputing TD-DFT oscillator strengths and confirming the gap moves <5%. Model: the same frozen FMs, plus (where available) an excited-state/optical head for a direct brightness readout; inference-only, probe from Experiment 1 reused. Systems compared: symmetry-breaking edit vs matched symmetry-preserving edit, per molecule. Decisive metric first: Symmetry-Break-vs-Preserve Causal Asymmetry = |change in the internal brightness signal under the symmetry-breaking edit| / |change under the matched symmetry-preserving edit|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 across the ~150 molecules with the brightness signal rising under symmetry breaking in >=70% of cases and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (both edits move the signal similarly -- a gap correlate). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as a qualified positive. Matched RMSD and verified near-fixed gap make any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means brightness does not respond to the symmetry change that the selection rule requires, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- parity/spin double dissociation): Strengthens clause (b) by checking the model reproduces the correct qualitative selection-rule structure, distinguishing two mechanisms an intensity-from-gap model cannot. Data: from the diagnostic subset, ~150 parity-forbidden (Laporte) transitions in centrosymmetric molecules and ~100 spin-forbidden (singlet-triplet) transitions, each with the symmetry-breaking edit from Experiment 2 (reused); reference TD-DFT confirms parity-forbidden transitions brighten under symmetry lowering while spin-forbidden ones stay dark. Model: frozen FMs with the brightness probe/head. Systems compared: parity-forbidden vs spin-forbidden classes under identical geometric symmetry breaking; shuffled-symmetry-label control. Decisive metric first: double-dissociation score = fraction of parity-forbidden transitions correctly predicted to brighten minus the fraction of spin-forbidden transitions incorrectly predicted to brighten. Convincing: score >= 0.5 (parity brightens, spin does not) with the shuffled-label control near 0. Refute: score <= 0.1 (the model cannot separate the two rules). Indeterminate band 0.1-0.5 (declared in advance): partial dissociation, reported without claiming a mechanistic separation. A negative result means the model does not distinguish parity from spin selection rules, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering an allowedness direction changes predicted absorption without moving the gap): Tests clause (c). Data: bright-vs-dark transition pairs and symmetric/symmetry-broken molecule pairs (from the sets above) used to recover the direction. Model: frozen FMs with excited-state/optical head; only the direction is fitted. We recover an 'allowedness/brightness' direction three ways -- supervised probe, SAE feature separating bright from dark, and a symmetry-broken-minus-symmetric delta -- and steer at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) allowedness direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a matched gap direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |predicted-absorption change under allowedness steering| / |mean change under random steering|; cross-talk = |gap shift under allowedness steering| / |gap shift under the gap direction|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, cross-talk <= 0.2 (brightness moves, gap barely does), and the gap direction moving the gap but not brightness -- a disentangled double dissociation replicated across the three recovery methods. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or cross-talk >= 0.6. Indeterminate band: selectivity 1.5-3 or cross-talk 0.2-0.6 (declared before the data): entangled/partial control, reported without a clean causal claim. A negative result means allowedness is not an independently steerable axis, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and selection-rule brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) across depth and models and places them on a spectrum. Data: QM8/QM9-spectra and the diagnostic subset (reused). Model: Uni-Mol/MACE and ChemBERTa-2, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered allowedness subspaces across models; (iii) upper bracket = a symmetry-aware transition-dipole model computing f from symmetry by construction, lower bracket = a gap-to-intensity regressor with no symmetry access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the gap-to-mechanism bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% bracket closure for at least one model AND cross-model CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the gap-regressor lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, reported without a universality claim. A negative result means no model exceeds a gap shortcut. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes/SAEs and public excited-state data, with reference TD-DFT only for the counterfactual geometries, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Oscillator strength and energy gap are correlated in typical datasets (accessible bright transitions dominate), making the brightness-beyond-gap separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with gap-residualization, the symmetry-breaking double-dissociation counterfactual (which holds the gap nearly fixed while varying symmetry), and the parity-vs-spin dissociation that a gap-correlate model cannot reproduce.

Constructing symmetry-breaking vs symmetry-preserving distortions with matched magnitude but different selection-rule consequences requires care with point-group assignment and verifying the intended brightness flip via reference TD-DFT; we compute reference oscillator strengths for the distorted geometries and report sensitivity to distortion magnitude and to point-group-assignment confidence.

Small geometric distortions may push conformers off the model's training distribution, confounding the symmetry-breaking response with generic out-of-distribution failure; we bound distortion RMSD, verify the gap stays nearly fixed, and compare against the matched symmetry-preserving distortion so any generic OOD effect is shared.

Many molecular FMs predict ground-state/scalar properties and may not natively output excited-state brightness; for these we probe whether the representation encodes brightness/selection-rule structure at all and prioritize models with excited-state or optical heads for the causal-steering readout, reporting per-model scope and treating scalar-only models as an informative lower bracket.

Excited-state reference data (TD-DFT oscillator strengths) is functional- and basis-set-dependent and noisy for weak transitions; we use curated consensus datasets (QM8, QM9-spectra), restrict decisive tests to well-characterized symmetric molecules, and emphasize the qualitative bright/dark flip over exact intensity magnitude.

Linear probes recovering an allowedness direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions—we use both probe directions and SAE features.

A negative result (models predict intensity as a gap correlate and fail the symmetry-breaking counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting molecular/materials FMs for photochemistry, OLED/dye, and optical-materials discovery, where symmetry-forbidden dark states are a central design consideration; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether foundation models represent optical selection rules.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public excited-state datasets (QM8, QM9-spectra), with reference TD-DFT for counterfactual geometries, keeping compute at academic scale.
